title: Polychromatic Colorings of Geometric Hypergraphs via Shallow Hitting Sets
abstract:
A range family ℛ is a family of subsets of ℝ^d, like all halfplanes, or all unit disks. Given a range family ℛ, we consider the m-uniform range capturing hypergraphs ℋ(V,ℛ,m) whose vertex-sets V are finite sets of points in ℝ^d with any m vertices forming a hyperedge e whenever e = V ∩ R for some R ∈ ℛ. Given additionally an integer k ≥ 2, we seek to find the minimum m = m_ℛ(k) such that every ℋ(V,ℛ,m) admits a polychromatic k-coloring of its vertices, that is, where every hyperedge contains at least one point of each color. Clearly, m_ℛ(k) ≥ k and the gold standard is an upper bound m_ℛ(k) = O(k) that is linear in k.
A t-shallow hitting set in ℋ(V,ℛ,m) is a subset S ⊆ V such that 1 ≤ |e ∩ S| ≤ t for each hyperedge e; i.e., every hyperedge is hit at least once but at most t times by S. We show for several range families ℛ the existence of t-shallow hitting sets in every ℋ(V,ℛ,m) with t being a constant only depending on ℛ. This in particular proves that m_ℛ(k) ≤ tk = O(k) in such cases, improving previous polynomial bounds in k. Particularly, we prove this for the range families of all axis-aligned strips in ℝ^d, all bottomless and topless rectangles in ℝ², and for all unit-height axis-aligned rectangles in ℝ².

      Abstract
A range family R is a family of subsets of Rd , like all halfplanes, or all unit disks. Given a range
family R, we consider the m-uniform range capturing hypergraphs H(V, R, m) whose vertex-sets
V are finite sets of points in Rd with any m vertices forming a hyperedge e whenever e = V ∩ R
for some R ∈ R. Given additionally an integer k ≥ 2, we seek to find the minimum m = mR (k)
such that every H(V, R, m) admits a polychromatic k-coloring of its vertices, that is, where every
hyperedge contains at least one point of each color. Clearly, mR (k) ≥ k and the gold standard is an
upper bound mR (k) = O(k) that is linear in k.
    A t-shallow hitting set in H(V, R, m) is a subset S ⊆ V such that 1 ≤ |e ∩ S| ≤ t for each
hyperedge e; i.e., every hyperedge is hit at least once but at most t times by S. We show for
several range families R the existence of t-shallow hitting sets in every H(V, R, m) with t being a
constant only depending on R. This in particular proves that mR (k) ≤ tk = O(k) in such cases,
improving previous polynomial bounds in k. Particularly, we prove this for the range families of
all axis-aligned strips in Rd , all bottomless and topless rectangles in R2 , and for all unit-height
axis-aligned rectangles in R2 .

 1      Introduction
We investigate polychromatic colorings of geometric hypergraphs defined by a finite set of
points V ⊂ Rd and a family R of subsets of Rd , called a range family. Possible range families
include for example all unit balls, all axis-aligned boxes, all halfplanes, or all translates of a
fixed polygon. In this paper we prove results for the following range families:
    the family RST = R1ST ∪ · · · ∪ RdST of all axis-aligned strips in Rd
    with RiST = {{(x1 , . . . , xd ) ∈ Rd | a ≤ xi ≤ b} | a, b ∈ R} for i = 1, . . . , d,
    the family RBL = {[a, b] × (−∞, c] | a, b, c ∈ R} of all bottomless rectangles in R2 ,
    the family RTL = {[a, b] × [c, ∞) | a, b, c ∈ R} of all topless rectangles in R2 , and
    the family RUH = {[a, b] × [c, c + 1] | a, b, c ∈ R} of all unit-height rectangles in R2 .
    For a fixed range family R and any finite point set V ⊂ Rd , the corresponding range
capturing hypergraph H = H(V, R) has vertex set V (H) = V , and a subset e ⊆ V is a
hyperedge in E(H) whenever there exists a range R ∈ R with e = V ∩ R. In this case, we
say that e is captured by the range R. That is, we have points in Rd and a subset of points
forms a hyperedge whenever these vertices and no other vertices are captured by a range.
For example, a set e of points in V ⊂ Rd forms a hyperedge in H(V, RST ) if and only if in at
least one of the d coordinates, the points in e are consecutive in V . (We assume throughout
that points in V lie in general position, i.e., have pairwise different coordinates.)

74:2   Polychromatic Colorings of Geometric Hypergraphs via Shallow Hitting Sets


           For a positive integer k, a k-coloring c : V → {1, . . . , k} of the vertices of a hypergraph
       H = (V, E) is called proper if each hyperedge e ∈ E contains at least two colors, i.e.,
       |{c(v) | v ∈ e}| ≥ 2, and polychromatic if each hyperedge e ∈ E contains all k colors, i.e.,
       |{c(v) | v ∈ e}| = k. Hence, proper 2-colorings and polychromatic 2-colorings are the same
       concept. However, if k ≥ 3, then every polychromatic k-coloring is also a proper k-coloring
       but the converse is not true in general. In fact, for polychromatic colorings we always seek
       to maximize the number of colors, as each polychromatic k-coloring, k ≥ 2, also gives a
       polychromatic (k − 1)-coloring by merging two color classes into one.
           For polychromatic colorings of range capturing hypergraphs with respect to a given
       point set V ⊂ Rd and range family R, we are particularly interested in the m-uniform1
       subhypergraph H(V, R, m) that consists of all hyperedges in H(V, R) of size exactly m.
       Instead of fixing m and then maximizing the k for which polychromatic k-colorings of
       H(V, R, m) exist, one usually considers the equivalent setup of fixing k and minimizing m.

       ▶ Definition 1. For a range family R and integer k > 0, let m = mR (k) be the smallest
       integer such that H(V, R, m) admits a polychromatic k-coloring for every finite set V ⊂ Rd .

           Clearly, mR (k) ≥ k since every hyperedge must contain k different colors. Moreover, we
       have mR (2) ≤ mR (3) ≤ · · · . But note that it is also possible that mR (k) = ∞ for some k.
       Namely this happens if for every positive integer m there exists a finite set of points V ⊂ Rd
       such that the corresponding hypergraph H(V, R, m) has no polychromatic k-coloring. In fact,
       throughout the over 40 years since their introduction by Pach [18, 19], we always observe the
       following surprising phenomenon for polychromatic k-colorings of geometric range spaces
       and the quantity mR (k) as a function of k: Either we already have that mR (2) = ∞, or the
       best known lower bounds are of the form mR (k) = Ω(k) for all k ≥ 2.

       ▶ Question 2. Is there a geometric range family R with mR (2) < ∞ and mR (k) = ω(k)?

          So, if the answer to Question 2 is ’No’, then we always have either mR (2) = ∞ or
       mR (k) = O(k). With this paper, we make progress on Question 2 by improving the upper
       bounds on mR (k) in several further cases from superlinear to mR (k) = O(k). We do so by
       proving a stronger statement, namely the existence of so-called t-shallow hitting sets with
       t = O(1); see Sections 1.1 and 1.2 below for the formal definition and a detailed discussion.

       1.1      Related work
       There is a rich literature on numerous range families R, polychromatic colorings of their
       range capturing hypergraphs, and upper and lower bounds on mR (k) in terms of k [2–4,7–11,
       13–17, 20, 21, 23, 24, 29]. Let us mention just a few here, while the interested reader is invited
       to have a look at the slightly outdated survey article [21] and the excellent website [1].

       (Some) known range families R with mR (k) < ∞ for all k ≥ 2.
       (1) For axis-aligned strips RST in Rd it is known that mRST (k) = Od (k log k) [3] and for
           d = 2 it is known that 3k/2 − 1 ≤ mRST (k) ≤ 2k − 1 [3].
       (2) For bottomless rectangles RBL in R2 it is known that 1.67k ≤ mRBL (k) ≤ 3k − 2 [4].
       (3) For halfplanes R in R2 it is known that mR (k) = 2k − 1 [29].
       (4) For axis-aligned squares R in R2 it is known that mR (k) = O(k 8.75 ) [2].

 (6) For translates of a convex polygon R in R2 it is known that mR (k) = O(k) [12].
 (7) For homothets of a triangle R in R2 it is known that mR (k) = O(k 4.09 ) [8, 14].
 (8) For translates of an octant R in R3 it is known that mR (k) = O(k 5.09 ) [8, 14].


 (Some) known range families R with mR (k) = ∞ for all k ≥ 2.
 (9) For unit disks R in R2 it is known that mR (2) = ∞ [20].
(10) For strips R in any direction in R2 it is known that mR (2) = ∞ [21].
(11) For axis-aligned rectangles R in R2 it is known that mR (2) = ∞ [11].
(12) For bottomless rect. and horizontal strips RBL ∪ R2ST we have mRBL ∪R2ST (2) = ∞ [10].

 Crucially, let us mention again, that in each of (1)–(8) the best known lower bound on mR (k)
 is linear in k, and it might be (in the light of Question 2) that in fact mR (k) = O(k) holds.

    One tool to prove for a range family R that mR (k) = O(k) are shallow hitting sets. For a
 hypergraph H = (V, E) and integer t > 0, a set X ⊆ V of vertices is a t-shallow hitting set if

      1 ≤ |e ∩ X| ≤ t       for every e ∈ E.

 That is, X contains at least one vertex of each hyperedge (X is hitting) but at most t vertices
 of each hyperedge (X is t-shallow). Shallow hitting sets for polychromatic colorings of range
 capturing hypergraphs have been used implicitly in [29], while being developed as a general
 tool in [7, 10, 15]. Clearly, for the m-uniform hypergraph H(V, R, m) taking X = V would be
 an m-shallow hitting set. But the challenge is to find t-shallow hitting sets with t = O(1)
 being a constant2 independent of m. If we succeed, this implies mR (k) = O(k).

 ▶ Lemma 3 (Keszegh and Pálvölgyi [15]). If for a shrinkable range family R there exists a
 constant t ≥ 1 such that for every m ≥ 1 every hypergraph H(V, R, m) admits a t-shallow
 hitting set, then mR (k) ≤ t(k − 1) + 1 = O(k).

     Here, a range family R is shrinkable if for every finite set of points V , every positive
 integer m and every hyperedge e in H(V, R, m) there exists a hyperedge e′ in H(V, R, m − 1)
 with e′ ⊆ e. Intuitively, we “decrease the size” of a range R ∈ R with R ∩ V = e until the
 first point of V drops out of the range. In fact, all range families mentioned in this paper,
 except the translates of a convex polygon (6) and unit disks (9), are shrinkable.
     Smorodinsky and Yuditsky [29] prove that every H(V, R, m) admits 2-shallow hitting sets
 for R being all halfplanes (3), which implies mR (k) ≤ 2k − 1 in this case. This is extended
 to so-called ABA-free hypergraphs in [15] and unions of hypergraphs in [10]. On the other
 hand, for the family RBL of all bottomless rectangles (2) the bound mRBL (k) ≤ 3k − 2 is not
 proven [4] by shallow hitting sets, and in fact it was asked [10, 15] whether these exist in this
 case. For R being all translates of a fixed convex polygon (6) the proof [12] for mR (k) = O(k)
 also involves shallow hitting sets, even though these are not explicitly stated as such, and
 this range family is not shrinkable anyways. Finally, the family R of all translates of an
 octant in R3 (8) is the only case for which shallow hitting sets are known not to exist [7],
 which follows from a certain dual problem for bottomless rectangles.

     Recall that m = mR (k) ≥ k is a growing function in k.

       1.2    Our results
       We consider the range families mentioned at the beginning of Section 1 of all axis-aligned
       strips RST in Rd , all bottomless RBL and all topless RTL rectangles in R2 , as well as all
       unit-height rectangles RUH in R2 . We remark that for the axis-aligned strips RST we could
       assume without loss of generality that these have unit-width. In this sense, unit-height
       rectangles are a generalization of horizontal strips. Additionally, unit-height rectangles are a
       generalization of bottomless and topless rectangles by “choosing the unit very large”. Thus,
       we can observe that mRUH (k) ≥ mR2ST (k) and mRUH (k) ≥ mRBL ∪RTL (k) hold for all k.
          Our main results are the following:
       Section 2. The family RST of all axis-aligned strips (1) in Rd allows for t-shallow hitting
          sets for some t = t(d) = O(d) (Theorem 5). This gives mRST (k) = Od (k), improving the
          Od (k log k)-bound in [3].
          We complement this with a lower bound construction       giving mRST (k) ≥ Ω(k log d)
          (Theorem 10). This greatly improves the mRST (k) ≥ 2 2d−1  2d · k − 1 lower bound in [3].
       Section 3. The family RBL of all bottomless rectangles (2) in R2 allows for 10-shallow hitting
          sets (Theorem 12). This answers a question of Keszegh and Pálvölgyi [15], as well as
          Chekan and Ueckerdt [10], and provides a new proof that mRBL (k) = O(k).
       Section 4. The family RBL ∪ RTL of all bottomless and topless rectangles (5) in R2 allows
          for 21-shallow hitting sets (Theorem 18). This already proves that mRBL ∪RTL (k) = O(k),
          which we improve to mRBL ∪RTL (k) ≤ 6k − 3 (Theorem 16).
          The family RUH of all unit-height rectangles allows for 63-shallow hitting sets, which
          already gives mRUH (k) = O(k) but can be improved to mRUH (k) ≤ 12k − 7 (Theorem 19).

       ▶ Remark. Most recently, we learnt about an unpublished manuscript of Rok, Schwartz,
       and Smorodinsky [28] concerning axis-aligned strips in Rd . They prove an upper bound of
       mRST (k) = O(kd), which is better than the Od (k log k)-bound in [3], but worse than our
       O(k log d)-bound in Section 2, as well as the same lower bound of mRST (k) ≥ Ω(k log d) as
       in Section 2. Apparently, these results also appear in the PhD thesis of Alexandre Rok [27].
       ▶ Remark. Let us also mention that Keszegh and Pálvölgyi [15] define a k-coloring c : V →
       {1, . . . , k} of a hypergraph H = (V, E) to be t-balanced if for any two colors i, j ∈ {1, . . . , k}
       and any hyperedge e ∈ E we have |{v ∈ e | c(v) = i}| ≤ t · (|{v ∈ e | c(v) = j}| + 1), i.e., any
       two colors appear roughly equally often in each hyperedge. They show that if a (shrinkable)
       range family admits t-shallow hitting sets then it also allows for t-balanced k-colorings for
       every k. And conversely, if we have t-balanced k-colorings for every k, then we have t2 -shallow
       hitting sets. Thus, Theorem 12 for example gives that every range capturing hypergraph
       H(V, RBL , m) for bottomless rectangles admits a 10-balanced k-coloring for every k ≥ 2.

       Notation. For an integer n ≥ 1 we sometimes use [n] = {1, . . . , n} for the set of the first n
       positive integers. Also, throughout this paper a hypergraph is a tuple H = (V, E) consisting
       of a finite set V of vertices (or points) and a finite multiset E of hyperedges, each being a
       subset of V . That is, hypergraphs may contain parallel hyperedges forming the same subset
       of vertices, sometimes called multiedges or hyperedges of multiplicity x for some x ≥ 2.

        2     Polychromatic Colorings for Axis-Aligned Strips
       For a shorthand notation, let us define md (k) = mRST (k) for the range family RST of all axis-
       aligned strips in Rd , d ≥ 2. As [3] pointed out, the problem of determining md (k) for RST can
       be seen purely combinatorial. That is, the problem of determining md (k) is equivalent to the
       following problem. Given a finite set V of size n and d bijections π1 , . . . , πd : {1, . . . , n} → V ,

we have to color the set V in k colors such that for each bijection πi , every md (k) consecutive
elements contain an element of each color. More formally, let k and d be positive integers.
Then, md (k) is the least integer such that for any finite set V of size n and any d bijections
π1 , . . . , πd : {1, . . . , n} → V , there exists a coloring c of V with k colors such that

   ∀x ∈ [k] ∀i ∈ [d] ∀a ∈ [n − md (k) + 1] ∃b ∈ [md (k)] : c(πi (a + b − 1)) = x.

   First, we list some known results for md (k).
   For d = 1 it is obvious that md (k) = m1 (k) = k for all k.
   For d = 2 it holds that 3k/2 − 1 ≤ md (k) = m2 (k) ≤ 2k − 1 for all k [3].
   For any d ≥ 2 it holds that md (k) ≤ k(4 ln k + ln d) for all k [3]. Thus, if d is a constant,
   then md (k) ≤ O(k log k).
   In [3] it is also proven that md (k) ≥ 2 · 2d−1

                                               2d · k − 1, while in [22] it is proven that for
   every k we have md (k) → ∞ as d → ∞.
    In this section, we show the existence of O(d)-shallow hitting sets for axis-aligned strips
in Rd . Moreover, we show an upper bound md (k) ≤ O(k log d), improving the result from [3],
and provide a lower bound of md (k) ≥ Ω(k log d).

2.1    Upper Bounds
Our upper bound uses a recent result about shallow hitting edge sets in regular uniform
hypergraphs. For a vertex v ∈ V in a hypergraph H = (V, E), the set of incident hyperedges
at v is denoted by Inc(v) = {e ∈ E | v ∈ e}. Hypergraph H is regular if | Inc(v)|, the degree
of v, is the same for all vertices v ∈ V . For an integer t ≥ 1, a subset M ⊆ E of hyperedges
is a t-shallow hitting edge set in H = (V, E) if we have

   1 ≤ |M ∩ Inc(v)| ≤ t       for every v ∈ V .

That is, 1-shallow hitting edge sets are exactly perfect matchings, while t-shallow hitting
edge sets for t ≥ 2 still cover each vertex at least once, but only at most t times. It turns
out, that all regular r-uniform hypergraphs admit t-shallow hitting edge sets with t only
depending on the uniformity r, and not on the number of vertices or their degree. Crucially,
this result even holds for r-uniform hypergraphs with multiedges, i.e., where two or more
hyperedges can correspond to the same set of r vertices.
▶ Theorem 4 (Planken and Ueckerdt [26]). Every r-uniform regular hypergraph H (with
possibly multiedges) has a t(r)-shallow hitting edge set with t(r) = er(1 + o(1)).
   Here, e = 2.71828 . . . denotes Euler’s number.
   Having Theorem 4, we find shallow hitting sets for axis-aligned strips as follows.
▶ Theorem 5. Let RST be the range family of all axis-aligned strips in Rd and m be a
positive integer. Then, for every finite point set V ⊂ Rd , the hypergraph H(V, RST , m) admits
a t(d)-shallow hitting set, where t(d) = 3ed(1 + o(1)).
Proof. Let V be a set of n points in Rd and let H = (V, E) = H(V, RST , m) be the
corresponding m-uniform range capturing hypergraph induced by axis-aligned strips in Rd .
We shall show that H has a t-shallow hitting set, where t = 3ed(1 + o(1)). Set r = ⌊m/2⌋. We
want to ensure that n is a multiple of r. To this end, if n = l (mod r) for some l ̸= 0, then
we add a set A of r − l new points, all of whose coordinates are larger than the coordinates
in V . Observe that if X ′ is a t-shallow hitting set in H(V ∪ A, RST , m), then X = X ′ ∩ V is
a t-shallow hitting set in H, since every e ∈ E is also a hyperedge in H(V ∪ A, RST , m).

       2.2     Lower Bounds
       We seek to give a lower bound on md (k) = mRST (k) for the range family RST of all axis-
       aligned strips in Rd . That is, for every d, k ≥ 1 we construct a point set V = Vd,k in Rd such
       that for some (hopefully large) m the range capturing hypergraph H(V, RST , m) admits no
       polychromatic k-coloring. Then it follows that md (k) ≥ m + 1. As a first step towards the
       desired point sets, we present a construction of r-uniform r-partite4 t-regular hypergraphs
       with t being relatively large in terms of r, which admit no (t − 1)-shallow hitting edge sets.

 5     Conclusions
In this paper, we extended the list of range families R for which the corresponding uniform
range capturing hypergraphs admit shallow hitting sets. This in particular implies that
mR (k) = O(k) for that family R, while mR (k) ≥ k always holds. In view of Question 2, it
would be interesting to investigate further range families R for which mR (k) < ∞ is known,
as to whether they admit shallow hitting sets. The current state of the art (for a selection of
range families) is summarized in Table 1.
